executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the accelerating tension between concentrated private power and public accountability — whether economic, technological, or institutional. The Economist's calculation of the 'MAGA tax' and the New York Times' coverage of intraparty conflict both point to a political economy under stress, where policy is increasingly shaped by factional loyalty rather than institutional consensus. Tech researchers suing the Trump administration over online safety, as covered in MIT Technology Review, extends this same fault line into the digital sphere, where the rules governing information and liability are being contested at the highest levels. SpaceX's financial disclosures add a corporate dimension to this story, raising questions about the transparency and oversight of a private entity with deep government entanglements. Taken together, today's content reflects a single underlying crisis: the established frameworks — regulatory, political, and financial — that once mediated between powerful actors and the public interest are visibly straining, and the outcomes of these contests will set the terms for the next era of American governance and markets.

newsletters.title: Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety

items.headline: Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety
items.blurb:
For months, the Trump administration has been going after researchers who study and try to counter hate speech, harassment, propaganda, and disinformation online. Now, some of those researchers are fighting back.

In a new lawsuit, they're seeking to strike down a visa restriction policy against "foreign officials and other persons" announced last year by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

They say the policy violates the speech and due process rights of foreign-born workers whose "work supports greater moderation of content on the [tech] platforms."

items.headline: Climate tech companies are pivoting to critical minerals
items.blurb:
We're over a year into the second Trump administration, and support for climate causes in the US is weak. But climate tech companies are finding ways to survive and even thrive in this new environment, including by looking beyond decarbonization.

One example is Boston Metal. The startup has raised a $75 million round to produce critical metals, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

The company is best known for its efforts to clean up steel production, an industry that's responsible for about 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the new focus and fresh funds could help it survive a period of waning support for industrial decarbonization.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
As the limits of LLMs become clearer, researchers are developing a new kind of AI designed to understand the physical environment: world models.

Recent developments from Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Yann LeCun's new startup have pushed these systems to the forefront of AI. At an exclusive virtual event today, MIT Technology Review will examine the progress—and what comes next.

newsletters.title: Money Talks: We calculate the MAGA tax

items.headline: What Donald Trump is costing the American economy
items.blurb: America's economy has become remarkably hard to read. Under Donald Trump, it can feel a bit like flying through crosswinds from all directions. Tariff whiplash, migration crackdowns, foreign "excursions" and policymaking chaos blow from one direction. The AI mania, soaring markets and fiscal largesse waft from another. Somehow, amid all this buffeting, economic growth has kept trundling along at around 2%. Holding America back is what we call the "MAGA tax". Our back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests the drag comes to just under one percentage point of growth a year. That works out to roughly $250bn annually, or about $730 per American.

items.headline: How fast America's economy should be growing
items.blurb: AI spending is helping, although perhaps less than many assume, because much of the hardware is imported and boosts Taiwan's GDP more than America's. We estimate that AI investment adds around 0.2 percentage points to growth, with frothy stockmarkets contributing another 0.3 points by making Americans a bit keener to spend by feeling much richer. Throw in tax cuts, easier dealmaking and other pro-business policies, and all this should be adding roughly 0.7 points to growth.

items.headline: Intraparty conflict: Republicans and Democrats fighting within their own ranks
items.blurb: Both political parties seem monolithic, and they gather more and more fervent support from their voters every year. Yet inside each is turmoil. Even as President Trump chases MAGA-skeptical Republicans from elected office, more than a third of G.O.P. voters want a new direction for their party, according to a new Times/Siena survey. At the same time, Democrats look strong in midterm election polls — even as their voters are miserable about the state of their party.

items.headline: Republican voters want a new direction, Times/Siena poll shows
items.blurb: Most Republicans still hold Trump as their lodestar. Only 37 percent of American voters approve of his performance, but three-quarters of Republicans and right-leaning independents do. But the poll showed that there are limits to fealty. Most Republicans under 45 think it was wrong to attack Iran, wrong to give Israel more economic and military support, wrong to focus so much on problems abroad.

items.headline: Democrats lead in midterm polls but voters are frustrated with their party
items.blurb: Registered voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republican ones by 10 points — a big lead! But that doesn't mean they like the party. More than half of Democrats and left-leaning independents vented their frustration in the poll.

newsletters.title: A title, an upset and revenge

items.headline: Bonjour, championnes — Montreal Victoire win the Walter Cup
items.blurb: In the PWHL, the Montreal Victoire are Walter Cup champions after a 4-0 rout of the Ottawa Charge. Montreal becomes the first Canadian champ in PWHL history, and caps a season of tremendous growth for the new women's pro hockey league. This will be a big summer for the league, with four expansion teams among the upcoming changes. Buy early.

items.headline: NHL upset: Golden Knights wallop Avalanche in Game 1
items.blurb: In the NHL, a surprise: The visiting Golden Knights walloped the star-laden Avalanche, 4-2, in Colorado. It should be noted the Avs were missing Cale Makar, but that doesn't fully explain how well Vegas played here.

items.headline: NBA: Oklahoma City ties series with Spurs after Game 2 rebound
items.blurb: And in the NBA, a rebound: Oklahoma City tied its battle of titans against the Spurs with a 122-113 win. MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was the difference, scoring 30 last night after a disappointing Game 1 performance. Two injuries to monitor: San Antonio's Dylan Harper left the game with a leg issue, while Oklahoma City's Jalen Williams exited with a reaggravated hamstring injury.

items.headline: The nagging worry of 24 — CFP expansion debate
items.blurb: Much like its basketball cousin, the tournament that started with four teams in 2014 and expanded to 12 teams two years ago now yearns for more games and more dollars. The Big Ten really, really wants that number to be 24. The SEC seems to prefer 16. There is fierce dissension about whether this is even worth it. The media numbers, both in terms of visibility and revenue, are huge with a 12-team Playoff, in which every team theoretically has a chance to win. Expand to 24, and it becomes a little less vital to watch a first-round game between two teams that might be 8-4.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Eli Lilly announced that an experimental drug has produced dramatic weight loss results, adding to the growing competition in the obesity treatment market [1]. The announcement marks a potentially significant development in a pharmaceutical sector that has seen surging demand for weight-loss medications in recent years.

Separately, SpaceX disclosed financial details revealing the extent of its profitability, underscoring the commercial strength of Elon Musk's rocket company [2]. The figures highlight how the private space industry has matured into a substantial revenue-generating enterprise, driven largely by SpaceX's dominance in launch services and satellite deployment.
